data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference is a 'betting quotient' distinct from probability: we bet on the corroborated theory not because it is likely true, but because the alternative (betting on a falsified one) is known to be wrong.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If there are infinite unconceived alternatives, making the 'only standing candidate' status meaningless.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'standing' candidate is actually false but hasn't been tested in the specific way that would reveal it (the problem of underdetermination).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a mere 'lack of disqualification' is indistinguishable in practice from acting on probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'asymmetric elimination'. Induction tries to prove the winner is right. Popper's approach merely proves the losers are wrong. When we prefer a corroborated theory, we are not saying 'this is probable'; we are saying 'all known alternatives have failed, so this is the only standing candidate.' This is a deductive state of affairs (A, B, C are false; D is not yet false; therefore, tentatively choose D). It avoids induction by refusing to assign positive weight to D, only negative weight to others. The cost is that we can never claim positive confidence, only a lack of disqualification, which feels psychologically and practically insufficient for high-stakes action.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
